title: Distributed Data Processing with Apache Spark
name: 11. Distributed Data Processing with Apache Spark
description: Master distributed computing fundamentals and large-scale big data processing with Apache Spark & PySpark: cluster architecture (Driver, Cluster Manager, Executors, Tasks), RDD lineage and fault tolerance, DataFrames, Datasets, Spark SQL and the Catalyst Optimizer, narrow vs. wide transformations, lazy evaluation, data partitioning (repartition vs coalesce), shuffle mechanics, broadcast joins, memory management (execution vs storage), data skew mitigation (salting, AQE), performance tuning with Spark Web UI, Parquet internals, Delta Lake Medallion Architecture (Bronze, Silver, Gold), and end-to-end distributed pipelines.

quiz.question: What is the primary difference between horizontal and vertical scaling in distributed computing?
options: Horizontal scaling increases CPU/RAM of a single machine; vertical scaling adds more nodes
Horizontal scaling adds more machines to the cluster; vertical scaling upgrades resources (RAM, CPU, NVMe) on a single machine
Horizontal scaling only works for relational databases
Vertical scaling requires Hadoop YARN
quiz.explanation: Vertical scaling (scaling up) upgrades the hardware capacity (CPU, RAM, storage) of a single node, whereas horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more commodity nodes to the cluster to distribute workloads in parallel.

quiz.question: How does Apache Spark achieve dramatic performance gains over traditional Hadoop MapReduce?
options: By eliminating network communication completely
By keeping intermediate data in memory across stages and utilizing directed acyclic graph (DAG) execution instead of writing intermediate states to disk
By replacing all Java code with C++ binaries
By only supporting single-threaded batch execution
quiz.explanation: Traditional MapReduce writes intermediate outputs to physical disks between Map and Reduce phases. Spark maintains reusable distributed datasets in RAM and executes optimized DAG plans, reducing disk and serialization bottlenecks.

quiz.question: What is the primary responsibility of the Spark Driver process?
options: Storing the physical HDFS blocks on disk
Running tasks and caching partitions on worker nodes
Coordinating application lifecycle, constructing logical and physical execution plans, and scheduling stages and tasks across executors
Managing cluster operating system updates
quiz.explanation: The Driver is the central coordinator of a Spark application: it interprets code, requests resources from the Cluster Manager, constructs DAG execution plans, divides jobs into stages/tasks, and coordinates executor task assignment.

quiz.question: What is a Spark Task?
options: An entire PySpark script executed from start to finish
The smallest unit of execution scheduled by the driver, processing a single partition of data within a stage
A cluster manager daemon running on Kubernetes
A physical CPU socket
quiz.explanation: A Task is the atomic unit of work scheduled by Spark's task scheduler. Each task runs on an executor core and processes exactly one partition of data for that stage.

quiz.question: How does an RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset) achieve fault tolerance without replicating all data partitions?
options: By continuously taking full snapshots of every partition to tape storage
By tracking transformation lineage, allowing any lost partition to be deterministically recomputed from base sources
By disabling node failures at the hardware layer
By forcing all operations to execute on the driver
quiz.explanation: RDDs maintain an immutable lineage graph recording the sequence of transformations used to create them. If an executor or partition is lost, Spark re-executes the lineage graph for that specific partition.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of DataFrames over raw RDDs for data engineering?
options: DataFrames run without a JVM
DataFrames are organized into named columns with a schema and benefit from Catalyst query optimizations and Tungsten execution code generation
DataFrames do not support SQL queries
DataFrames cannot be partitioned
quiz.explanation: Unlike untyped low-level RDDs where Spark treats data as opaque Java/Python objects, DataFrames possess structured schemas that allow the Catalyst Optimizer to prune unused columns, push down predicates, and generate optimized bytecode via Project Tungsten.

quiz.question: What does Predicate Pushdown achieve in Spark SQL?
options: Pushes all sorting operations to the driver
Applies filter conditions directly at the data storage layer (e.g. Parquet row groups) before loading records into memory
Converts DataFrames into unstructured text files
Increases the number of shuffle partitions
quiz.explanation: Predicate pushdown delegates filtering expressions (such as `WHERE amount > 5000`) to the underlying storage format (like Parquet or database connectors), skipping irrelevant blocks and minimizing disk I/O and network transfer.

quiz.question: Which of the following is considered a wide transformation in Apache Spark?
options: map()
filter()
select()
groupBy()
quiz.explanation: Wide transformations (like groupBy, distinct, join, orderBy) require data from multiple input partitions to be redistributed across the network to compute final groupings. In contrast, narrow transformations (like filter, select, map) operate independently within existing partitions.

quiz.question: Why does Apache Spark evaluate transformations lazily?
options: Because Python cannot execute code synchronously
To allow Spark to inspect the entire DAG of transformations and build a globally optimized physical execution plan before executing any data scans
To prevent any data from being written to disk
To ensure Spark only executes on a single CPU core
quiz.explanation: Lazy evaluation allows Spark's Catalyst engine to analyze the full chain of transformations, combining adjacent filters, eliminating unused columns, and choosing optimal join algorithms before triggering cluster compute on an action.

quiz.question: What is the difference between repartition() and coalesce()?
options: repartition() can only decrease partitions; coalesce() can only increase partitions
repartition() performs a full shuffle across the cluster to balance data; coalesce() avoids a full shuffle and is typically used to reduce partition counts
coalesce() requires a cluster restart
repartition() writes all data to local disk
quiz.explanation: repartition() redistributes data evenly across a specified number of partitions using a full cluster shuffle. coalesce() merges adjacent partitions without a full shuffle, making it much more efficient when reducing partition counts (e.g. before saving output files).

quiz.question: Why is a Spark Shuffle considered one of the most expensive cluster operations?
options: It forces the driver to restart
It involves disk I/O serialization, network transfer across worker nodes, deserialization, and sorting of intermediate partition blocks
It disables parallel processing
It requires all worker machines to have identical GPU hardware
quiz.explanation: A shuffle requires mappers to write partition files to disk, transfers massive volumes of data across the network switches between worker nodes, and forces reducers to deserialize and sort records by key before computing aggregations.

quiz.question: When is a Broadcast Join optimal in Spark SQL?
options: When joining two multi-terabyte fact tables
When joining a large table with a relatively small lookup/dimension table that fits comfortably in executor memory
When both tables have severe data skew on the join key
When the network connection between workers is completely disconnected
quiz.explanation: A broadcast join copies the small dimension dataset to every executor once, allowing each executor to join its local large-table partitions without triggering an expensive full-table network shuffle.

quiz.question: How does Salting resolve data skew during large-scale aggregations or joins?
options: By deleting records associated with the popular key
By appending random suffixes (salts) to high-frequency keys to evenly distribute their rows across multiple worker partitions
By compressing the dataset with gzip
By moving all calculations to the driver
quiz.explanation: Salting adds an artificial random integer (e.g. 0-9) to heavily skewed keys (like 'Mumbai_3'), spreading the single massive bottleneck key across multiple independent tasks before final reconciliation.

quiz.question: Under Spark Unified Memory Management, how do Execution Memory and Storage Memory interact?
options: They use completely separate static hardware RAM chips with no sharing
They share a unified region; execution can evict storage blocks if memory is required for active shuffles/joins, but storage cannot evict active execution memory
Storage memory always terminates running execution tasks
Neither memory region can ever spill data to disk
quiz.explanation: Under Unified Memory Management, execution and storage share a dynamic memory pool. If execution memory needs space for joins or sorting, it can evict cached storage blocks to disk, ensuring active tasks do not fail unnecessarily.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between raw Apache Parquet files and a Delta Lakehouse table?
options: Parquet is row-based; Delta Lake is column-based

Parquet is an immutable columnar storage file format, whereas Delta Lake adds an ACID transaction log (_delta_log), schema enforcement, time travel, and UPDATE/MERGE/DELETE capabilities on top of Parquet files
Delta Lake cannot be read by Apache Spark
Parquet files require an external relational database server
quiz.explanation: Parquet is a raw columnar storage file format. Delta Lake is an open lakehouse storage layer that encapsulates Parquet files with an ACID transaction log, offering atomic commits, time travel, schema evolution, and merge capabilities.
